guides.title: Lascaux and the Vézère Valley
guides.description: Upper Paleolithic cave art, the evidence for its age, and the landscape around the original cave and its replicas.
guides.intro: Above the Vézère River in southwestern France, painters and engravers used a limestone cave to make images of horses, aurochs, stags and other animals. The chambers preserve a sequence of artistic choices. Bones and tools on the cave floor supply a different record of the people who went underground.
guides.scope: Upper Paleolithic art and visits to the original cave, with nearby archaeological sites and the history of discovery, conservation and replication. Ages in calibrated years before present use 1950 as the reference year.

map.scope: Modern terrain in the Dordogne, from Montignac-Lascaux to Les Eyzies and the surrounding Vézère valley. Markers are approximate and include both the original cave and modern replicas.

paragraphs.text: The protected landscape reaches well beyond the Lascaux hill. The World Heritage property groups 15 components, including caves, open rock shelters and sites known for deposits left by people. At Le Cap Blanc, sculpted animals project from a rock shelter wall. Paint and engraving at Font-de-Gaume show another combination of techniques. The valley brings these records into geographic proximity, even though people used its sites over many different periods.

Lascaux’s entrance stands roughly 110 metres above the valley floor. Inside, the available passages branch through the limestone for a combined length of about 235 metres. The ministry’s cave plan follows the passage from the entrance through the broad Hall of the Bulls, then shows the branches and lower chamber where other groups of images survive.

At the entrance end, the Hall of the Bulls opens into the Axial Gallery. Their pale calcite surfaces reflect light and give strong contrast to broad painted figures. Elsewhere the texture of the rock differs, and the Apse is densely engraved. The cave’s overall plan helps make sense of the shift in scale and technique from one surface to the next.

Where a painted contour crosses another, specialists can sometimes work out which figure was put down first. In the Hall of the Bulls, an early group of dark horses preceded the large aurochs, and some small stags were added later. Paint composition offers a second line of evidence for changes in technique. These observations establish a relative order for individual figures. The time between painting episodes remains uncertain.

People carried light into the inner cave. Archaeologists recovered lamps, including a shaped sandstone example from the Shaft. Finds of portable objects and stone tools open a second window onto activity underground, alongside the marks that survive on the walls.

sections.heading: Dating a visit and dating a painting

paragraphs.text: Radiocarbon dates refer first to the material sampled. Researchers dated five reindeer remains from different sectors of Lascaux to around 21,500–21,000 calibrated years before present, near the transition between the Badegoulian and early Magdalenian archaeological traditions. The result is evidence for human visits that left material on the floor. A connection between these visits and particular paintings remains open.

Earlier measurements on reindeer antler suggested an older age for some material, and stylistic comparisons have supported different attributions. Calibration also changes the numbers readers encounter in older accounts. A laboratory age is expressed in radiocarbon years and must be calibrated to estimate elapsed calendar time.

paragraphs.text: Marcel Ravidat, Georges Agniel, Simon Coencas and Jacques Marsal entered the cave in September 1940. Public visits began in 1948. The first guides reported green algae in the late 1950s, and the state closed the original to the public in 1963. Conservation now treats the cave and its surroundings as a system whose environment requires continuing observation.

Lascaux II opened in 1983 with copies of the two large painted spaces near the former visitor entrance. The International Centre of Cave Art opened Lascaux IV in 2016 as a much more extensive reproduction. The three locations sit close together. The wider valley map places them in their landscape, while the cave plan shows the arrangement of rooms underground.

guides.title: The Roman Empire
guides.description: A Mediterranean-wide guide to Roman expansion, provincial life and the empire’s transformation in Late Antiquity.
guides.intro: Roman power reached across Europe, North Africa and western Asia. From Rome to Alexandria, Carthage, Palmyra and Constantinople, people experienced it through different institutions and ways of life. These sites show how imperial rule changed over time and why the history of Rome has several turning points.
guides.scope: The late Republic and Roman Empire, with emphasis on the first centuries of imperial rule and on changes from the third to seventh centuries CE. The medieval eastern Roman Empire appears in outline through 1453.

map.scope: Modern terrain and approximate landmarks from Britain to the eastern Mediterranean. Sites belong to different periods of Roman rule and its successors.

sections.heading: How republican expansion became imperial rule

paragraphs.text: Rome governed subject territories well before it had an emperor. Republican armies and diplomacy established provinces around the Mediterranean. In the last century BCE civil wars transformed who held power at Rome. Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE, took control of Egypt in 30 BCE, and received the name Augustus from the Senate in 27 BCE. The last of these events is the conventional start of the imperial period.

Augustus later claimed that he had returned public affairs to the Senate and people. His account presents the new order through the ruler’s own eyes. Augustus retained decisive power and republican titles and institutions remained in use. The early imperial arrangement is often called the Principate, from the emperor’s position as Rome’s leading citizen.

Subjects encountered the empire in the demands of soldiers, tax collectors, local authorities and courts, and in opportunities offered by commerce or military service. The same imperial system could leave quite different local records. At Dendur in Egypt, Augustus appears in the visual role of a pharaoh in a temple honoring Egyptian gods and two local figures. Farther north, a bronze military diploma is evidence of how service in the Roman army could confer citizenship before Caracalla’s broader grant in 212 CE.

The Mediterranean made long-distance movement possible, while harbours, roads and settlements organized who and what could move. The evidence for a sea journey, a road segment or a commercial community comes from different sources. An excavated harbour records the infrastructure that made shipping possible. Inscriptions and goods reveal particular links, while researchers combine archaeological and documentary evidence to reconstruct a wider road system.

A single object can capture more than one kind of connection. The gravestone of Regina, found at South Shields in northern Britain, records a woman connected with a British people and a man from Palmyra. Its two inscriptions use Latin and Palmyrene Aramaic. The monument gives a human scale to the empire’s geographic extent and to the migrations and legal relationships discussed in the linked studies.

The empire had more than one political center by Late Antiquity. Constantinople was dedicated in 330 CE and became the enduring eastern capital. The western court moved to Ravenna in 402. In the fifth century, armies and kingdoms took over parts of the West. Some successor rulers continued to govern through institutions and elites inherited from the empire. The change looked different from one province to the next.

The removal of Romulus Augustulus in 476 marks the end of a western imperial court in Italy. The eastern court continued to rule from Constantinople, and in the sixth century it reestablished direct control in parts of the former West. The eastern state, often called Byzantium, endured through further territorial losses, recovery and a period of exile before the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453.

sections.heading: Following the evidence across three studies

paragraphs.text: The frontiers study begins where Roman administration met the terrain, from Britain’s stone and turf barriers to a bridge and fort in Dacia. The cities study follows the infrastructure and people that sustained exchange. The Late Antiquity study traces power through Ravenna, Carthage and Constantinople, where changes in government left different archaeological and artistic records.

guides.title: Roman Expansion and Frontiers
guides.description: How conquest, bridges, garrisons and local settlements shaped the outer provinces of the Roman Empire.
guides.intro: At Birdoswald, the Roman army placed a fort above a river. In Dacia, a bridge and fort helped secure a crossing of a much larger river, the Danube. These were different answers to local terrain, military priorities and the movement of people and goods.
guides.scope: The late Republic through the third century CE, with case studies in Britain, Dacia, North Africa and Syria.

map.scope: Modern terrain with approximate locations of selected forts, crossings, colonies and cities. The dated locations illustrate different forms of Roman control.

points.label: Rome
points.description: The Senate granted Octavian the title Augustus in Rome. It is the conventional starting point for the imperial period.

points.label: Birdoswald on Hadrian’s Wall
points.description: The fort at Banna occupied a ridge over the River Irthing. Its remains include the stone fort and evidence of an earlier turf wall.

points.label: Drobeta
points.description: Roman fort and remains of Trajan’s bridge at the Danube crossing by present-day Drobeta-Turnu Severin.

points.label: Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa
points.description: The Roman provincial colony in Dacia stood at a different site from the earlier Dacian royal center, Sarmizegetusa Regia.

points.label: Timgad
points.description: Trajan’s colony on the northern side of the Aurès in modern Algeria had a planned street grid, forum and civic buildings.

points.label: Palmyra
points.description: An oasis city in modern Syria, with strong commercial ties across the Roman and Iranian frontier zones.

paragraphs.text: Imperial conquest extended a system of provincial rule built during the Republic. Augustus inherited an empire in this geographic sense. Under Claudius, the invasion of Britain in 43 CE began the conquest of what became the Roman province there. Trajan’s war in Dacia brought land north of the lower Danube under Roman control in 106. Different dates mark the campaign, the creation of a province and the work of keeping it supplied.

Trajan also took territory in his war against Parthia. The extent reached late in his reign was short-lived. His successor Hadrian abandoned much of the new eastern territory. The brief advances and later withdrawals matter when reading a map labeled with a single year. Cities such as Palmyra could remain part of Roman Syria while maintaining relationships across the Euphrates with people under other rulers.

Work on Hadrian’s Wall began around 122 CE. Its design changed during building, and forts were incorporated into the system. Excavations at Birdoswald distinguish an early turf barrier from subsequent stone building. The fort itself occupied high ground over a river and housed troops. The remains show how a wall line connected to a larger landscape of posts, routes and settlements.

Controlled crossings and observation mattered alongside defense. Later building and occupation altered the frontier again. The stone visible at any one locality represents part of that history, and English Heritage’s site accounts distinguish features built at different times.

sections.heading: The Danube and the Dacian uplands

paragraphs.text: At Drobeta, a fort and the remains of Trajan’s bridge mark a connection across the Danube. The Dacian limes farther inland combined legionary and auxiliary forts, temporary camps, watchtowers and earthworks. In a landscape broken by hills and valleys, sites helped control approaches to the province and access to resources such as gold and salt.

The Dacian royal center at Sarmizegetusa Regia lay in the Orăștie Mountains. The Roman colony with the name Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa was founded at a separate site. Archaeological remains of the two places record different political centers. The Roman system north of the river lasted into the later third century, and the UNESCO account dates the operation of the Dacian limes to 106–271 CE.

The North African colony of Timgad had a planned grid and a forum. Founded under Trajan, it illustrates a civic form of imperial expansion in the Aurès region. In Britain, a frontier fort and the communities near it depended on connections for food, goods and labor. Military diplomas show one way long service could affect the legal status of auxiliaries. These forms of settlement and mobility were part of governing the provinces.

guides.title: Roman Cities, Trade and People
guides.description: Harbours, streets, inscriptions and letters show how goods moved and how people lived across the Roman world.
guides.intro: A harbour basin near Rome, a shop in Pompeii, a carved face at Palmyra and a letter from Vindolanda preserve different kinds of evidence. Together they show the work, institutions and relationships behind the movement of goods and people.
guides.scope: Urban and everyday life in the first three centuries CE, from Mediterranean ports and a Syrian oasis to the communities of northern Roman Britain.

sections.heading: A coastal port for an inland city

paragraphs.text: Rome stood inland on the Tiber. In the first century CE Claudius built a harbour near the river’s mouth, and in the early second century Trajan added a sheltered, six-sided basin to the complex. Quays, canals and storage buildings organized the transfer of cargo between seagoing ships, warehouses and smaller vessels bound up the river. Excavation at Portus also records the people who worked, lived and were buried around this industrial landscape.

Samples from Portus preserve a changing story of food supply. The excavation team suggests that early third-century workers consumed wheat and olive oil brought from North Africa. Pottery and other finds show more North African products in later deposits. Egypt was another grain supplier to Rome, and Alexandria had a long history as a Mediterranean harbor. These sources reveal different parts of the supply system, including what reached the port and what workers themselves ate.

Roads and shipping linked ports to different inland markets. Travel time depended on the kind of transport, terrain and season. The Itiner-e atlas brings archaeological traces and written evidence together and records different degrees of confidence in road alignments. A surviving stretch of paving can support part of a route, while the stretch between excavated points may be reconstructed from other evidence.

sections.heading: Two kinds of city on commercial networks

paragraphs.text: Floods, eruptions and subsequent excavation shape which buildings can be studied. Pompeii offers an exceptional street-level record because of the Vesuvius eruption of 79 CE. Shops opposite the Stabian Baths opened onto a busy part of the city. Their relationship to streets and public buildings helps place trade within the daily life of a neighborhood.

Palmyra grew around an oasis in the Syrian Desert. Merchants and caravans linked it with settlements in Roman Syria and with territories toward and beyond the Euphrates. Funerary reliefs tell another part of its history. The portraits and inscriptions marked family tombs and communicated names and relationships in locally meaningful ways. They preserve the choices of individual families in a multilingual provincial city.

A funerary portrait from early imperial Rome may represent a man who had been freed from slavery. Such objects give uneven access to the past: people who could commission a portrait are easier to see than many of the enslaved people whose labor supported Roman households and businesses. The sculpture’s setting and comparison with inscribed reliefs help historians interpret who it may portray.

Military service was one route to citizenship for some noncitizens. Bronze diplomas record grants to qualifying individuals. In 212 CE Caracalla’s edict extended Roman citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire. A fragmentary Greek copy preserved on papyrus is an unusually direct witness to that imperial decision. Enslavement and distinctions of wealth and social rank persisted.

At Vindolanda, an invitation from Claudia Severa asks Sulpicia Lepidina to attend a birthday celebration. The wooden tablet preserves the domestic and social lives of officers’ households near a northern garrison. It is an unusually intimate document, surviving alongside other letters and accounts from the site.

sections.heading: Artifacts and what they can tell us

paragraphs.text: A harbour, a letter and a legal document answer different scales of question. Portus shows how cargo could be handled, the Vindolanda tablet records a relationship between two people, and the citizenship edict captures a change intended to reach almost the whole free population.

What social ties connected households around the northern garrison communities?
How could an inland capital handle large quantities of seaborne cargo?

guides.title: Late Antiquity and the Eastern Roman Empire
guides.description: Changes of rule in the West, continuity at Constantinople, and the changing place of North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean.
guides.intro: Ravenna, Carthage and Constantinople followed different paths through the fifth and sixth centuries. Ravenna passed from a western imperial court to Ostrogothic and eastern Roman rule. Constantinople sustained a Roman imperial government for centuries after the western court disappeared.
guides.scope: The third through seventh centuries CE, especially Italy, North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean, with an outline of eastern Roman continuity to 1453.

map.scope: Modern terrain and approximate urban sites. The markers show places where imperial continuity and political change took different forms.

points.label: Rome
points.description: Rome retained political and religious importance even as imperial courts moved elsewhere. The city was sacked twice in the fifth century.

points.label: Ravenna
points.description: Court city of the late western empire, later an Ostrogothic royal seat and a center of eastern Roman administration in Italy.

points.label: Carthage
points.description: Carthage became the capital of the Vandal kingdom and later the center of eastern Roman government in Africa.

points.label: Alexandria
points.description: A major city in the eastern Roman province of Egypt, Alexandria passed to Muslim rule during the seventh-century conquests.

points.label: Constantinople
points.description: Constantine’s imperial city occupied the site of Byzantium, on the Bosporus at modern Istanbul.

paragraphs.text: Emperors in Late Antiquity governed through different courts. Under Diocletian, a four-ruler arrangement known as the Tetrarchy distributed imperial responsibilities. Constantine later established his imperial city at Byzantium, on the Bosporus between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Dedicated in 330 CE, Constantinople became the durable seat of the eastern Roman court. The western court established itself in Ravenna in 402.

Christianity gained imperial support under Constantine, and later emperors strengthened its standing. Changes in official policy left time and space for considerable religious diversity. Fourth- to seventh-century communities around the Mediterranean included several Christian traditions as well as Jewish communities, and the pace of change varied across the provinces.

sections.heading: The end of the western court in Italy

paragraphs.text: The Vandals captured Carthage in 439, taking a major North African city from the western empire. In 476 the military commander Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in Italy. Historians use 476 to mark the end of the western imperial court in Italy. Governance in the former western provinces developed through different arrangements, as rulers worked with locally rooted elites and legacies of imperial institutions.

The Christian monuments of Ravenna span successive governments. The Mausoleum of Theodoric recalls an Ostrogothic ruler. San Vitale preserves portraits of Justinian and Theodora in mosaic from the era of restored imperial control. Their proximity makes government under different rulers visible in the same urban landscape.

Rome’s maritime port preserves the changing economic setting. Researchers at Portus found evidence for a decline in some North African imports after the fifth century and suggest food supplies became more reliant on sources closer to Rome. The excavations show changes in consumption over several generations, including the years after the Vandal sack of Rome in 455.

In 533 Justinian launched a campaign against the Vandal kingdom in North Africa. Eastern Roman forces took Carthage and later reestablished imperial rule in Italy after prolonged war. The reconquests placed new demands on a state whose military interests also extended east. In Constantinople, construction of the present Hagia Sophia under Justinian gave the capital a new imperial church.

Justinian also ordered the assembly and revision of major collections of Roman law. The Codex arranged imperial enactments for use by the government and legal practitioners. In Ravenna a mosaic could represent the power of an emperor ruling across the Adriatic. The legal compilation shows a different kind of reach, through rules carried in texts and applied by officials.

sections.heading: Territorial change and a longer eastern history

paragraphs.text: By the start of the seventh century, Syria, Egypt and North Africa included many of the eastern empire’s wealthiest provinces. During and after the seventh-century conquests they passed under Islamic rule at different times. Objects gathered in The Met’s Age of Transition exhibition trace the continuation of trade, craft and religious life amid that change. A silver plate showing the biblical battle of David and Goliath, dated 629–630, combines a Christian subject with figures in late Roman military dress.

Byzantine is a modern convention for the eastern Roman Empire. Its people called themselves Romans. The imperial state centered on Constantinople continued with changing territory, a large Greek-speaking population and shifting political institutions. Crusaders took the capital in 1204. An eastern Roman government recovered it in 1261, and the Ottomans took it in 1453.

guides.title: Hadrian’s Wall
guides.description: The Tyne–Solway frontier, its forts and crossing points, and the communities whose lives continued around it.
guides.intro: From Wallsend on the Tyne to Bowness on the Solway Firth, Hadrian’s Wall crossed river valleys, uplands and low coastal ground. Its curtain wall was one part of an evolving system of fortifications, roads and communities that can still be traced through excavation and surviving earthworks.
guides.scope: Northern Roman Britain, from the start of construction around 122 CE through the late Roman period and evidence of later occupation at Birdoswald. The guide map covers the Tyne–Solway corridor.

map.scope: Modern terrain and approximate archaeological locations. Follow the sites from the Solway coast in the west to Wallsend on the Tyne in the east.

points.label: Bowness-on-Solway (Maia)
points.description: The westernmost fort of the wall occupied a low rise over the Solway Firth. Most remains are buried beneath the modern village.

points.label: Birdoswald on Hadrian’s Wall
points.description: The fort at Banna occupied a ridge over the River Irthing. Its remains include the stone fort and evidence of an earlier turf wall.

points.label: Poltross Burn Milecastle 48
points.description: This gated fortlet preserves a short stretch of stairway and traces of its interior buildings.

points.label: Housesteads (Vercovicium)
points.description: An upland fort whose excavated remains include barracks, granaries and a communal latrine.

points.label: Chesters (Cilurnum)
points.description: Cavalry fort near a crossing of the North Tyne. Remains include a riverside bathhouse.

points.label: Wallsend (Segedunum)
points.description: The eastern end of the wall at a fort overlooking the River Tyne.

paragraphs.text: Construction began on Hadrian’s orders around 122 CE. Military roads and forts already served the region, including along the Stanegate to the south of much of the new line. Legionaries built much of the frontier. Plans changed as the work went on, including the addition of forts directly on the line and an eastward extension to Wallsend. The western part initially used turf in stretches later rebuilt in stone.

The completed curtain ran for roughly 80 Roman miles, about 117 kilometers, between Wallsend and Bowness-on-Solway. Beyond the western end a chain of military installations extended down the Cumbrian coast. The frontier used ridges, rivers and shorelines as well as constructed barriers. Ground plans and excavations reveal its course where the standing wall has disappeared.

sections.heading: Gates, towers, forts and the Vallum

paragraphs.text: Regularly spaced gateways occupied small fortified enclosures known as milecastles. Two smaller turrets generally stood between neighboring milecastles. At Poltross Burn, the surviving stair steps help archaeologists estimate the level of an upper walkway. At Chesters, fortifications overlooked the North Tyne crossing, and excavated structures include a bathhouse down by the river.

A ditch lay north of the wall where the ground called for one. The Vallum lay to the south and consisted of a broad ditch with banks. Its causeways channeled movement through the military zone. A road known as the Military Way linked installations behind the curtain in a later phase. These features show how the army used depth, communication and controlled passage along the line.

cells: Garrison buildings, riverside baths and evidence of the bridge crossing nearby.
Gateways, part of a stair and the remains of interior buildings.
An earlier turf wall, Roman fort buildings and later timber construction.
Separate earthworks and roads shown alongside the wall on regional archaeological plans.

paragraphs.text: Farmers lived in northern Britain before the wall went up, and farmsteads and settlements continued around the military zone. Excavation near Brampton preserves traces of enclosed Romano-British farmsteads. Near the forts, civilians lived close to military households. The archaeological record captures some of the people moving across long distances into this region as well as people with local roots.

At South Shields, beyond the wall’s eastern end, a gravestone commemorates Regina. Its Latin text identifies her as a woman of the Catuvellauni and the freedwoman and wife of Barates, who was from Palmyra in Syria. A second inscription uses Palmyrene Aramaic. One surviving object thus records enslavement, freedom, marriage and migration in the society around the frontier.

In the 140s CE Antoninus Pius pushed the frontier north to the Forth–Clyde line, building the separate Antonine Wall. About two decades later Roman forces returned to Hadrian’s Wall and brought installations back into use. The frontier continued to be rebuilt and occupied through the later Roman centuries.

Birdoswald gives unusually detailed evidence for the period after formal Roman rule in Britain ended. Excavations found timber structures built over parts of the Roman fort, including former granary areas. This sequence shows continued use of the site and a change in the form of occupation. Archaeologists infer how the new buildings may have functioned from their postholes and relationship to the former fort.

cells: Construction of Hadrian’s Wall begins across northern Britain.
A new frontier is established farther north under Antoninus Pius.
Roman forces return to the Tyne–Solway frontier and restore installations.
Late Roman and early medieval periods
The fort at Birdoswald preserves evidence of occupation and subsequent timber buildings.

guides.title: Stonehenge and Its Landscape
guides.description: The stone circle, earthworks and burial monuments of Salisbury Plain, and what the stones reveal about their origins.
guides.intro: On Salisbury Plain, Stonehenge stands among burial mounds and the remains of paths, enclosures and timber circles. Farming communities made and revisited these places over many generations. Archaeological surveys reveal their relationships in the landscape, while geological studies trace some of the stones to distant sources.
guides.scope: The Neolithic and Early Bronze Age around Stonehenge in Wiltshire, including earlier earthworks, several phases at the stone circle and evidence for three distinct groups of stone. Avebury is the separate northern component of the World Heritage property.

map.scope: Modern terrain and approximate landmarks in the Wiltshire landscape around Stonehenge, Woodhenge, Durrington Walls and the River Avon.

points.label: Stonehenge stone circle
points.date: Earthwork about 3000 BCE; major stones about 2500 BCE
points.description: The circular earthwork and surviving stones belong to a sequence of construction and rearrangement.

points.label: Greater Cursus
points.description: Approximate point along a long rectangular earthwork north of Stonehenge. Its bank and ditch extend nearly three kilometers.

points.label: Stonehenge Avenue
points.description: A point along the route defined by banks and ditches that links the monument to the River Avon.

points.label: Durrington Walls
points.description: Archaeology within and around this large enclosure records houses, timber structures and gatherings.

points.label: Woodhenge
points.description: Concentric rings of postholes record a timber monument near Durrington Walls. Modern markers show where the posts stood.

points.label: New King Barrows
points.description: Burial mounds on the ridge east of Stonehenge form part of a wider pattern of cemeteries around the monument.

sections.heading: An earthwork before the stone circle

paragraphs.text: The Greater Cursus to the north was already ancient when the major stone settings went up. Its bank and ditch enclose a long strip of chalk downland. Early Neolithic communities also built long barrows in the area. These works leave clues to gathering and burial across Salisbury Plain well before the most familiar stages of Stonehenge.

Around 3000 BCE people dug a circular ditch and formed banks. A ring of pits known as the Aubrey Holes belongs to the early history of the site, and cremated human remains have been found in and around the earthwork. Around 2500 BCE builders raised the large sarsens, constructing a circle with lintels and a horseshoe of taller paired uprights. Subsequent work rearranged smaller stones within the enclosure.

cells: The Greater Cursus and other early Neolithic monuments predate the earliest ring at Stonehenge.
The circular ditch and bank define an early phase. Cremations show that people buried some of their dead there.
The main sarsen settings take shape. Nearby Durrington Walls preserves evidence of late Neolithic houses and gathering.
Bluestones were rearranged and the Avenue linked the circle and the Avon in English Heritage’s phased timeline.
Early Bronze Age round barrows added burial places across the surrounding landscape.

sections.heading: Houses, timber rings and a route to the river

paragraphs.text: At Durrington Walls, floors and postholes mark houses, while pottery and animal bones record food preparation and large gatherings. Some houses were occupied around the time of the major work at Stonehenge. English Heritage presents a connection with the builders as an archaeological interpretation. Nearby Woodhenge shows another form of monument, recognizable through the arrangement of postholes left by its timbers.

The Avenue runs from the circle toward the River Avon. Near Stonehenge its alignment corresponds to midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset along the monument’s principal axis. The link to the river and the solar alignment are visible relationships. The ceremonies that may have used the route and the meanings participants attached to them remain matters of interpretation.

sections.heading: What the stones say about their sources

paragraphs.text: Chemical analyses show that 50 of the 52 sampled surviving sarsens belong to a closely similar group. A core from one of the uprights matches stone from West Woods in the Marlborough Downs, making that area a likely source for most of the large sarsens. Geological comparisons trace several of the smaller bluestones, including types of dolerite and rhyolite, to the Preseli area of west Wales.

The flat sandstone known as the Altar Stone has a different geological history. In 2024, researchers compared the ages and chemistry of mineral grains and matched it to rocks of the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland. A 2026 follow-up found the closest age matches in Caithness sandstone and assessed possible glacial dispersal, alongside the need for substantial human transport. The precise source outcrop and itinerary remain unresolved.

Round barrows at New King Barrows and elsewhere on the downs brought new burials into view of older monuments. The surrounding area spans thousands of years of construction, burial and alteration. The local terrain map places individual sites in relation to the Avon and the chalk ridges. The linked historic landscape maps show the scale of the earthworks and why Avebury is treated as a separate component of the same World Heritage property.
